strengths: Significance: DiscoGen addresses a useful infrastructure gap by providing configurable algorithm-discovery tasks across ten ML domains. Separating editable modules, datasets, backends, and objectives supports controlled experiments that would otherwise require substantial engineering.

Soundness: The within-task meta-train/meta-test distinction is well motivated. Generating the meta-test filesystem after discovery and restoring fixed files are sensible safeguards. The baseline comparisons, per-dataset results, and module-combination experiments provide useful evidence about current agents’ reliability and transfer failures.

Originality: The contribution is primarily a reusable synthesis of procedural task generation and modular algorithm discovery. Its configurable search spaces and explicit nested evaluation structure offer useful experimental capabilities without requiring a new discovery algorithm.

Presentation and transparency: The main framework is clearly explained, and the appendices provide extensive task descriptions, prompts, dataset splits, and computational costs. The manuscript acknowledges unsuccessful runs, benchmark contamination risks, and economic, environmental, and misuse concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness—prompt optimisation: Section 7 does not establish that optimisation improves over the original prompt under matched conditions. Table 3 compares only optimised prompts, while Table 2 uses different action budgets (Appendix E.1). Only one final prompt per task-count setting is reported, without independent optimisation repetitions that capture task-sampling and prompt-search variability. Consequently, the monotonic aggregate result is insufficient evidence for a reliable diversity-scaling effect; the separate suites in Table 9 are not monotonic.

Soundness—evaluation separation: Excluding exact DiscoBench configurations does not exclude exposure to their underlying evaluation datasets. Figure 4 shows prompt optimisation using Asterix and SpaceInvaders feedback, which are also DiscoBench meta-test environments. More concretely, Appendix N.3.1 passes 'Best meta-test (Asterix ~31)' into the discovered ADA prompt, despite Appendix N.2 explicitly prohibiting disclosure of meta-test datasets. This contradicts the claimed hidden-dataset separation for that experiment. The paper needs an exposure audit and a clearer distinction between unseen configurations and unseen datasets.

Soundness—ranking and uncertainty: The Elo procedure makes any increase in successful attempts dominate algorithm performance, but exempts baseline comparisons from this rule (Section 5.1; Appendix E.2). Thus the headline ranking mixes reliability and solution quality asymmetrically. The bootstrap sampling unit and handling of dependent datasets and shared discovery runs are unspecified. Separate reliability and quality summaries, a transparent failure policy, and hierarchical uncertainty estimates are needed to make the rankings dependable.

Significance and evidential scope: The roughly 493 million tasks count configurations of a relatively small collection of datasets and modules; it does not establish comparable semantic diversity. Appendix I estimates task correlations using only three agents and one baseline, without uncertainty or a noise control. Rank reversals among four systems cannot establish low redundancy across the generator. The evidence supports a useful configurable task collection, but not the stronger claims of near-indefinite optimisation with low overfitting risk.

Reproducibility and technical consistency: Although open-source release is claimed, the supplied manuscript provides no identifiable DiscoGen repository or executable artifact. There is also a concrete discrepancy in the showcased language-model loss: Appendix O.6 specifies logits shaped [batch, sequence, vocabulary] and padding labels of -1, whereas Example 2 scatters labels and applies softmax along dimension 1 without masking padding. It requires an undocumented reshaping/filtering adapter to satisfy that interface. This example needs reconciliation and reproducible quantitative results before supporting the discovery claims.

Construct validity: Most measured headroom concerns producing executable implementations, and Appendix K provides only two examples selected for strong meta-test performance, without controlled comparisons or component ablations. Combined with the failure-dominated scoring, this leaves insufficient evidence that the benchmark distinguishes algorithm-discovery ability from implementation reliability—the distinction used to motivate it. An implementation-only baseline and systematic analysis of successful discoveries would materially strengthen the contribution.

strengths: Significance: DiscoGen addresses a useful infrastructure gap: generating configurable algorithm-discovery tasks across ten ML domains. Editable modules, alternative backends, and separate development and evaluation datasets make the framework potentially valuable for studying discovery agents.

Soundness: The explicit inner-loop, meta-loop, and agent-optimisation distinctions are valuable. Generating the meta-test filesystem only after discovery and restoring fixed modules are sensible measures against accidental leakage and evaluation modification (Sections 4.1–4.2).

Evaluation: The paper provides substantial descriptive evidence, including three discovery runs per model/task, per-dataset results, an until-success analysis, and all 15 module combinations for on-policy RL. Reporting failures and baseline superiority candidly helps characterize current agent limitations.

Originality and presentation: The contribution is primarily a useful integration of procedural task construction and cross-dataset algorithm evaluation, rather than a new discovery algorithm. The main exposition explains this integration clearly. Appendices provide prompts, dataset splits, interfaces, and compute estimates; the impact statement discusses misuse, access, environmental costs, and labour effects.
weaknesses: Soundness—prompt-optimisation evidence: Section 7 reports one resulting prompt per task-count setting, without reported independent repetitions of the entire optimisation process. Consequently, task diversity is confounded with the particular sampled domains, tasks, and optimisation trajectory. Table 3 also lacks an untuned-prompt control under the same evaluation budget; Table 2 is not directly comparable because Appendix E specifies different action budgets. The results suggest a benefit but do not establish reliable improvement from procedural task diversity.

Soundness—scoring and uncertainty: Appendix E.2 makes any model with more successful attempts dominate one with fewer attempts, regardless of successful-run performance, while exempting baseline comparisons from this penalty. This mixes implementation reliability and algorithm quality under different comparison rules. The bootstrap resampling unit and treatment of dependencies among datasets, tasks, and discovery seeds are unspecified. Separate reliability and conditional-quality summaries, domain-balanced aggregation, and a fully specified uncertainty procedure are needed to interpret the headline Elo results.

Significance—effective diversity remains insufficiently established: Equation 1 correctly counts configurations, but hundreds of millions of dataset partitions and module combinations do not themselves establish comparably broad discovery problems. Appendix I estimates task correlations using only three models and a baseline, all models sharing the same agent scaffold, without uncertainty or repeatability analysis. Noisy rank reversals cannot by themselves establish low redundancy. The framework's breadth is credible, but the claimed effective scale needs stronger validation.

Evaluation boundaries: Excluding exact DiscoBench configurations from prompt optimisation does not establish independence from their constituent datasets and modules. Appendix E samples from the same domain-specific dataset pools, potentially exposing benchmark meta-test datasets through other optimisation tasks. This can be legitimate evaluation within a shared task distribution, but it should be distinguished from transfer to genuinely unseen datasets or domains. Public datasets and hidden split identities also do not justify the stronger contamination-resistance claims, particularly the suggestion that a future private API would solve contamination.

Construct validity and reproducibility: Most failures are attributed to syntax errors or hardcoded shapes, and only one agent scaffold is evaluated. Thus, the benchmark currently measures a substantial implementation-robustness component; the claim that modular tasks better isolate research ability needs evidence, such as matched baseline-initialisation and conventional tuning controls. Despite extensive appendices, the manuscript provides no identifiable DiscoGen repository link or version supporting its open-source claim, and details such as the precise failure penalty remain incomplete. These gaps, rather than the honestly acknowledged resource limitations, prevent a stronger recommendation.

strengths: Significance: DiscoGen provides useful infrastructure for algorithm-discovery research across ten ML domains. Configurable editable modules, dataset assignments, and initialisations support systematic experiments beyond a fixed collection of manually authored tasks.

Soundness: Separating algorithm development from evaluation on hidden meta-test datasets is a substantive design strength. Generating the meta-test filesystem only after discovery and restoring fixed modules provide concrete protections against direct evaluation leakage (Sections 4.1–4.2).

Empirical contribution: Three language models, three discovery seeds, per-dataset results, and the exhaustive on-policy RL module-combination experiment provide informative evidence about implementation reliability and transfer. The paper candidly reports that agents generally underperform standard algorithms.

Originality: The contribution is primarily the integration of procedural task configuration, modular algorithm discovery, and nested evaluation into a reusable framework. This is a meaningful systems and benchmark contribution even though its individual ingredients are established.

Presentation and reproducibility: The loop definitions and configuration example are clear. Appendices document dataset splits, agent budgets, prompts, task sampling, compute usage, and discovered code. The impact statement substantively discusses misuse, labour, accessibility, and environmental costs.
weaknesses: The headline task count measures configurations, not independent research problems. Appendix I estimates task correlations from only three models and a baseline, using one agent scaffold and success-conditioned results. Ranking changes can reflect statistical noise as well as meaningful task differences. These analyses support some diversity but do not establish low redundancy across hundreds of millions of configurations.

The prompt-optimisation evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive (Section 7). Independent optimisation trajectories and task-sampling repeats are not reported, so task identity and optimisation randomness are confounded with task count. There is no untuned-prompt comparator under the same evaluation budget; Table 2 uses different budgets. Consequently, Table 3 establishes relative performance among the resulting prompts, not a reliable improvement over the original ADA or a general scaling relationship.

The aggregate metric obscures algorithm quality. Appendix E.2 makes any advantage in successful-run count dominate performance differences between agents, while exempting baseline comparisons. This blends reliability and quality using different comparison rules. The bootstrap resampling unit and dependence handling are also unspecified. Reporting reliability separately from unconditional utility and conditional algorithm quality would make the conclusions easier to assess.

Generalisation and contamination claims need tighter qualification. Excluding exact DiscoBench configurations from ADA optimisation does not exclude their constituent datasets, modules, or related tasks. Procedural recombination of a public finite dataset pool reduces direct exposure to particular evaluations but does not eliminate contamination or establish transfer to genuinely unseen research settings. The proposed private API is future work.

Evidence for discovering substantively new algorithms is limited: Appendix K presents two examples selected for strong meta-test performance without controlled ablations or further held-out confirmation. Combined with frequent syntax and compatibility failures, the current evaluation substantially measures implementation competence. This does not invalidate the benchmark, but limits claims about research creativity and scientific discovery.

The ethical discussion is thoughtful, but restricting editable files and selecting beneficial task domains do not establish that optimising discovery agents avoids broader capability gains or misuse. Those safety claims should be framed as hypotheses. Overall, the useful benchmark contribution supports weak acceptance, while these evidential limitations prevent a stronger recommendation.

strengths: Significance: DiscoGen provides useful infrastructure across 14 ML domains. Configurable editable modules, dataset splits, backends, and initialisations enable controlled studies that are difficult with fixed task suites.

Soundness: Separating algorithm development from evaluation on held-out datasets is appropriate for measuring algorithm transfer. Generating the meta-test filesystem after discovery and restoring fixed modules are sensible safeguards (Sections 4.1–4.2).

Evaluation: Three models, repeated discovery runs, per-dataset results, module-count sweeps, and initialisation comparisons establish that the framework is operational and exposes meaningful performance differences. The additional successful-run analysis shows that baseline superiority is not explained solely by invalid submissions.

Originality and presentation: The contribution is primarily a useful synthesis of procedural task generation and modular algorithm discovery. The distinction between inner-loop, meta-loop, and agent optimisation is clearly explained, and the appendix supplies extensive configurations, prompts, discovered code, and compute information.

Limitations and ethics: The paper acknowledges restricted agent coverage, computational expense, and remaining contamination risks. Its impact statement discusses misuse, environmental costs, and access barriers; no concrete material ethical violation is evident.
weaknesses: Soundness—agent optimisation: Table 4 lacks an untuned-prompt control under the same evaluation budget. Appendix C gives prompt-tuning evaluation fewer actions than the main DiscoBench experiments, preventing a clean comparison with Table 3. Independent repetitions of the prompt-optimisation process are not reported, so task-sampling and optimisation variability remain unmeasured. The held-out-domain confidence intervals overlap substantially. These results suggest a benefit from broader exposure but do not convincingly establish robust optimisation gains or scaling.

Soundness—diversity: Approximately 99 billion configurations are not equivalent to independently informative discovery problems; roughly 98% arise from the MARL domain. Appendix F computes task correlations using only three models and a baseline, without establishing ranking reliability. Changing rankings can reflect stochastic noise, and cannot by itself substantiate the claimed low redundancy of the combinatorial space or near-indefinite optimisation without overfitting.

Evaluation validity: Elo gives any agent with more successful runs precedence over one with fewer, regardless of solution quality, while baseline comparisons follow a different rule. This makes the headline metric difficult to interpret as algorithm-discovery performance. Appendix C does not specify the bootstrap resampling unit or adequately address dependence among tasks sharing datasets. Separate reliability and conditional-quality summaries, with sensitivity analyses, would make the conclusions more trustworthy.

Contamination and generalisation: Hiding a task's meta-test selection does not remove prior exposure to its public datasets or known algorithms. Appendix E also places related datasets, such as CIFAR-10 and its corrupted or long-tailed variants, across the boundary. The safeguards improve evaluation, but the stronger contamination-resistance claims require qualification and an explicit audit of dataset relationships.

Reproducibility and presentation: Despite substantial documentation, exact scoring and uncertainty procedures remain underspecified. Domain descriptions also conflict with Table 2: Appendix A lists six off-policy RL modules versus seven in the table, and four on-policy RL modules versus six. These discrepancies affect reconstruction of the advertised task space.
Overall: The framework has clear practical merit, but the evidence supporting its central diversity and agent-improvement claims needs strengthening before the stated conclusions can be relied upon.

strengths: Significance: DiscoGen addresses a useful infrastructure gap: generating configurable algorithm-discovery problems with separate development and held-out evaluation datasets. Its integration of 14 domains, editable modules, alternative initialisations, and evaluation objectives could support substantial future research.

Originality: The contribution is primarily the unified task-generation framework and evaluation design, rather than a new discovery algorithm. Combining modular search spaces with explicit inner-loop, meta-loop, and agent-optimisation boundaries is a worthwhile contribution.

Soundness: The empirical evaluation includes three open-weight models, three discovery runs per setting, per-dataset results, and additional successful-run analysis. Appendix I.2 shows that the baseline remains stronger even after excluding failed submissions, providing useful evidence that implementation reliability alone does not explain the performance gap.

Presentation and reproducibility: Figure 1 clearly explains the nested evaluation structure. The appendices provide task splits, prompts, sampling procedures, agent budgets, and compute estimates. The manuscript acknowledges restricted model coverage, the limited scope of prompt tuning, and future contamination risks. Its impact statement meaningfully discusses misuse, environmental costs, accessibility, and human oversight; I see no demonstrated material ethical violation.
weaknesses: Soundness—prompt-optimisation claims: Section 7 does not report independent repetitions of the complete prompt-optimisation process for each task-count setting. Consequently, task identity, task order, and stochastic prompt generation are confounded with task count. The evaluation confidence intervals do not establish robustness across optimisation runs, and the held-out-domain intervals overlap substantially. Table 4 also lacks an untuned-prompt control under the same evaluation budget; Table 3 uses different action budgets according to Table 5. The results suggest a promising trend but do not establish reliable improvement over the original agent or a general scaling relationship.

Soundness—effective diversity: Equation 1 counts configurations, not independent discovery challenges. Approximately 98% of the advertised task count comes from On-Policy MARL, and many configurations reuse the same datasets and code. Appendix F assesses diversity using rankings of only three agents and a baseline, conditioned on successful runs, without quantifying ranking uncertainty. Low correlations could partly reflect estimation noise. This analysis does not substantiate the stronger claims of low redundancy across the enormous generated task space or near-indefinite optimisation with little overfitting.

Evaluation validity: The Elo procedure makes any additional successful run dominate arbitrary performance improvements, while exempting baseline comparisons from that rule. This combines reliability and algorithm quality through a consequential, asymmetric preference. Although success rates and the successful-run analysis help, sensitivity to this aggregation choice is missing. Appendix C.2 also does not identify the bootstrap resampling unit or explain how dependence among datasets and tasks sharing discovery runs is handled.

Construct validity: Much of the observed difficulty concerns producing executable implementations: Table 3 reports only 17.8–40.5% success on All Edit tasks, and Section 5.2 attributes failures to syntax errors and hardcoded shapes. This is useful diagnostic evidence, but it weakens the claim that the benchmark isolates research ability from software engineering. The two hand-selected examples in Appendix H lack controlled comparisons or component ablations establishing discovery beyond recombination of known techniques. A systematic analysis of successful improvements over baseline would strengthen the benchmark's interpretation.

Contamination claims exceed the demonstrated protection: Generating meta-test files after discovery is a useful safeguard against direct access, but recombining public datasets and established algorithms does not rule out prior exposure to their data or solutions. The statement that prepublication evaluation is therefore uncontaminated is too broad. The proposed private API is future work, and no contamination audit supports the stronger comparative claims.

Reproducibility and presentation need correction: Some domain specifications conflict: Table 2 lists six On-Policy RL modules and seven Off-Policy RL modules, whereas Appendices A.12 and A.9 describe four and six respectively. Appendix A.6 specifies perplexity for language modelling, while the corresponding results plot validation accuracy. These discrepancies affect task reconstruction and score interpretation. Overall, the framework has clear merits, but the central claims about scalable learning and effective task diversity require stronger controls and uncertainty analysis before acceptance.

strengths: Significance: DiscoGen addresses a useful problem: providing configurable tasks for developing algorithm-discovery agents, with explicit separation between algorithm development and evaluation on held-out datasets. Its implementation across 14 domains is a substantial infrastructure contribution.

Originality: The contribution lies in combining modular algorithm interfaces, configurable dataset splits, initializations, and objectives into a reusable task generator. This is a meaningful benchmark-design contribution even without a new discovery algorithm.

Soundness: The evaluation includes three open-weight models, three discovery runs per task, per-dataset results, and additional successful-run analyses. Table 7 shows that the human baseline remains stronger even after conditioning on successful submissions, providing useful evidence beyond simple execution failure rates.

Presentation and reproducibility: The nested optimization loops are clearly explained. Appendices document dataset splits, agent budgets, task sampling, prompts, generated algorithms, and compute expenditure. These details substantially support reproducibility, alongside the stated open-source release.

Limitations and ethics: The paper acknowledges contamination, computational costs, limited agent coverage, and the restricted scope of prompt optimization. Its impact discussion addresses misuse, environmental costs, and access barriers; no material ethical violation is evident.
weaknesses: Soundness of the optimization claims: Table 4 compares four optimized prompts without a matched untuned-prompt control. Table 3 cannot directly supply that control because the action budgets differ (Appendix C.1). Independent repetitions of the complete prompt-tuning process are not reported, leaving task-sampling and optimization variability unquantified. The held-out-domain confidence intervals overlap substantially. The results suggest a benefit from broader task exposure but do not establish reliable optimization gains or a scaling relationship.

Evaluation-boundary inconsistency: Appendix K.2 instructs the prompt optimizer not to reveal meta-test datasets, but the one-task prompt in K.3.1 explicitly states 'Best meta-test (Asterix ~31)' and incorporates associated performance guidance. Asterix also appears in DiscoBench's on-policy RL meta-test split. Using meta-test feedback for outer-loop optimization is legitimate, but transferring these identities and results into the evaluated ADA contradicts the stated hidden-dataset boundary. The overlap should be audited and results reported with affected evaluation tasks excluded; this concern does not by itself invalidate the four held-out domains.

Diversity claims exceed the evidence: Equation 1 counts configurations, not independent discovery problems, and approximately 98% of the advertised configurations come from MARL. Appendix F infers semantic diversity from rankings of only three agents and a baseline, using a selected subset with successful runs. Ranking changes can also arise from stochastic variation. Without repeatability estimates or uncertainty analysis, these correlations do not establish low redundancy across billions of tasks. Likewise, decreasing average success with module count in one domain does not establish a generally smooth difficulty landscape.

The headline metric complicates interpretation: Appendix C.2 makes any improvement in submission success count dominate algorithm quality in agent-to-agent comparisons, while baseline comparisons receive different treatment. This measures a particular preference for robustness rather than algorithm performance alone. The bootstrap resampling unit and handling of dependencies between datasets and tasks are insufficiently specified. Separate validity and conditional-performance rankings, with sensitivity to aggregation choices, would make the conclusions more dependable.

Construct validity remains limited: Most experiments use empty initialization, and the manuscript attributes many failures to syntax errors and hardcoded shapes. Consequently, substantial benchmark variation reflects implementation competence, despite the motivation to distinguish research ability from software engineering. The baseline-initialization experiment is helpful but limited, while two selected algorithm examples do not establish systematic discovery beyond known methods. Overall, the infrastructure has clear merits, but the generalization and diversity claims need tighter evidence before acceptance.
